Issued at 210 AM EDT Sat Oct 31 2106

             -----------Synoptic Overview-----------

Mid-level ridging is parked atop the Sunshine State this morning. A
broad area of above-normal H5 heights extends over the eastern half
of the U.S. In the polar jet stream, a shortwave over New England
is responsible for reinforcing a continental high-pressure system
over the Great Lakes. In the West, a longwave trough axis sits 
just offshore of California. Additional shortwave energy, on the 
nose of the subtropical jet, is located over Texas.

By Sunday evening, the surface high should move into the
Mid-Atlantic, tightening the pressure gradient over Florida yet
again. Meanwhile, the mid-level shortwave currently over Texas is 
expected to reach the northeastern Gulf and/or Florida. Guidance 
has continued to trend slower with the arrival of this feature. A 
surface reflection, most likely in the form of a weak trough, may 
attempt to form over the eastern Gulf by Sunday evening. Enhanced
low-level moisture convergence is anticipated to coincide with a 
broad area of upper-level jet diffluence, especially from Sunday 
night into Monday morning. During this period, total moisture 
(PWAT) is forecast to exceed the 90th percentile of climatology 
over Florida.

This disturbance is forecast to weaken by Tuesday as it crawls
eastward. By Wednesday night, cluster analysis of the 30/12Z
ensemble suite shows another shortwave trough axis approaching the
Mississippi Valley. With additional jet stream energy on its heels,
guidance suggests this trough will begin to weaken as it reaches
the Southeast U.S. on Thursday. This portends a rather unimpressive
cold frontal passage for Florida sometime on Thursday. Somewhat
drier air is still likely to reach the state once it passes.

The subtropical jet is forecast to become quasi-zonal over the
Southern U.S. late next week and into the following weekend. Global
ensembles indicate a weak ridge developing near Florida, maintaining
above-normal H85 (5 kft) temperatures. The next signal appears
to be a southern stream trough entering the Desert Southwest next
weekend. It is not expected to reach Florida until at least Monday
the 9th.

             -------Sensible Weather & Impacts-------

Today - Tonight...

Unfortunately, high-res guidance has struggled with the pesky band
of showers that has remained over portions of the Treasure Coast the
last 12 hours or so. We expect that periodic showers will continue
to stream off of the Atlantic, especially for areas south of Cape
Canaveral today. Rain chances range from 10-30% northwest of I-4
to 50-60% from Melbourne southward. Lightning chances remain low
(<25%). Showers that repeatedly affect the same areas may drop 1-3"
on a very isolated basis, so we will continue to monitor trends
for localized flooding.

East-northeast winds increase a bit today as the gradient tightens
up. Expect occasional gusts from 20-30 mph this afternoon. This
will continue to generate rough surf and numerous, life-threatening
rip currents at Atlantic beaches. A High Surf Advisory will go 
into effect at 5 PM today. Please refrain from entering the ocean.
Minor to moderate coastal flooding is also expected with the 
midday high tide mainly from near St. Lucie Inlet and points 
southward into Martin County.

Warm and muggy today with highs in the low/mid 80s.

Sunday - Monday...

As mentioned in the overview, several factors favor widespread
coverage (60-80%) of showers with a few storms (20-30%). Sunday may
not be a washout for all of the area, however, as the disturbance
responsible for the active weather is moving in a bit slower. We
anticipate the greatest areal coverage of rain sometime later
Sunday through midday Monday.

The influx of energy and moisture, combined with frictional
convergence and some instability emerging off the Atlantic, favor
the I-95 corridor for training bands of heavy rain. To make matters
worse, much of the Treasure Coast is nearly saturated from recent
rains. Through Monday night, most likely rainfall tallies of 1
to 3 inches are forecast for much of east central Florida, with a
5-10% chance of localized 5" or greater totals. Where these higher
amounts fall in a shorter timeframe, flash flooding could result.

Easterly winds will be strongest on Sunday, with gusts up to 30
mph. The High Surf Advisory remains in effect on Sunday at all
Atlantic beaches of Central Florida. Additionally, another round of
minor coastal flooding is forecast south of St. Lucie Inlet with 
the early afternoon high tide cycle, especially on Sunday. The 
high risk of life-threatening rip currents will persist into early
next week.
